posts.author: The Decoder
posts.text: FTC launches sweeping probe into OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs over consumer protection concerns. The FTC is formally investigating OpenAI, Anthropic, and other leading AI labs over potential consumer protection violations. The agency plans to force document handovers and executive testimony through legally binding demands. The probe was already underway before the Hugging Face hack and goes well beyond the FTC's earlier push to hold companies liable for their agents' behavior. posts.text: Google drops Gems for Skills, joining OpenAI and Anthropic in the shift to agent-ready prompt formats. Google is replacing Gems with "Skills" in Gemini chat. Skills are detailed, reusable prompts that users invoke by typing "/" or that Gemini runs automatically. The format is based on an open standard from Anthropic. Gems will be phased out starting in November, with existing ones migrating automatically. posts.text: Google Gemini 4 Argon closes the gap with OpenAI and Anthropic but doesn't take a clear lead. Gemini 4 Argon is Google's first frontier model in over seven months. It matches GPT-6 Astra in independent testing but can't keep up with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. The per-token price is low, but Argon burns through more than twice as many tokens per task as Astra. Select testers get access first, with the API and paid tiers following later. posts.text: Trump and tech CEOs sign an AI code of conduct that's only "morally binding". President Trump and tech leaders including Mark Zuckerberg, Greg Brockman, Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk signed an AI code of conduct at the White House that is only "morally binding." Outside auditors are supposed to check whether models work as intended. It's unclear what would happen if a company broke the rules. Trump also signed an executive order renaming AI "Super Intelligence." The article Trump and tech CEOs sign an AI code of conduct that's only "morally binding" appeared first on The Decoder .

posts.text: Trump tells federal agencies to use the term 'Super Intelligence ' instead of artificial intelligence. President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing all federal agencies to stop using the term 'artificial intelligence' and instead call it 'Super Intelligence.' The president said that the new term will solve AI's branding issue and that it 'more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.'

posts.text: Google is paying almost no publishers almost nothing for content used in AI answers. Google pays about 100 digital publishers for content used in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to The Information. Payments range from under $1,000 over several months to more than $1 million a year. Some participants don't know how Google calculates payments, while some larger publishers are holding out for higher rates.
